> Demo document for the fictional CF Bank. Illustrative content only, not legal advice.

# AML/CFT policy

## 1. Purpose and scope
This policy sets out how CF Bank manages the risk that it is used for money laundering or terrorist financing. It applies to every business line, to all employees, and to agents and outsourced providers acting for the bank.

It is supported by procedures for customer due diligence, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reporting and record keeping.

## 2. Governance
- The Executive Committee ensures that policies and controls match the bank's risk exposure and are implemented.
- The Compliance Officer runs the policies, procedures and controls day to day, is the contact point for supervisors and transmits reports to the FIU.
- Approval of this policy and of the business-wide risk assessment stays with the bank and is never outsourced.

## 3. Business-wide risk assessment
The Compliance Officer drafts the business-wide risk assessment each year and the Executive Committee approves it.

## 4. Risk-based approach
- Customers are assigned a risk tier at onboarding using the scoring model owned by Compliance.
- Standard due diligence applies to all customers; enhanced measures apply to higher-risk customers and PEPs, as set out in the EDD and PEP procedure.
- The decision on a customer's risk profile is taken by an employee of the bank, never by a provider.

## 5. Monitoring and reporting
Transactions are monitored against what the bank knows about the customer. Detection criteria are approved by the Compliance Officer. Staff escalate suspicions as described in the suspicious-transaction reporting procedure.

## 6. Monitoring this policy
Compliance tests the controls on a schedule set in the controls library. Deficiencies are logged with an owner and a due date until closed. The Compliance Officer reports significant weaknesses to the Executive Committee.

## 7. Approval and review
This policy is approved by the Executive Committee member responsible for compliance and reviewed every 24 months.

# AML/CFT policy

## 1. Purpose and scope
This policy sets out how CF Bank manages the risk that it is used for money laundering or terrorist financing. It applies to every business line, to all employees, and to agents and outsourced providers acting for the bank.

It is supported by procedures for customer due diligence, enhanced due diligence and PEPs, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reporting, record keeping and training.

## 2. Governance

- Approval of this policy and of the business-wide risk assessment stays with the bank and is never outsourced.

## 3. Business-wide risk assessment
The Compliance Officer drafts the business-wide risk assessment each year. The Executive Committee approves it. It is refreshed earlier when a new product, channel, technology or customer segment is launched, or when an internal or external event changes the bank's exposure.

## 4. Risk-based approach
- Customers are assigned a risk tier at onboarding using the scoring model owned by Compliance.
- Standard due diligence applies to all customers; enhanced measures apply to higher-risk customers and PEPs, as set out in the EDD and PEP procedure.

## 6. Sanctions
The bank applies targeted financial sanctions and takes measures against the risk of non-implementation and evasion, as described in the sanctions screening procedure.

## 7. Training and integrity
Staff complete role-based training and confirm that they have read this policy at each new version. Staff in AML/CFT roles are assessed before they start and at regular intervals.

## 8. Monitoring this policy
Compliance tests the controls on a schedule set in the controls library. Deficiencies are logged with an owner and a due date until closed. The Compliance Officer reports significant weaknesses to the compliance manager.

# Customer due diligence procedure

## 1. Purpose and scope
Step-by-step onboarding and ongoing due diligence for retail and business customers of CF Bank. It is run by Onboarding, with Compliance as second line.

## 2. When due diligence applies
1. When a business relationship is established.
2. For an occasional transaction above the applicable threshold.
3. Whenever money laundering or terrorist financing is suspected, whatever the amount.
4. When there are doubts about previously collected identification data.
5. When there are doubts about whether the person you deal with is the customer or an authorised representative.

## 3. Identification and verification
| Customer type | Minimum data | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| Natural person | Name, date of birth, nationality, address | Identity document check, liveness check |
| Legal entity | Legal name, registration number, registered address, representatives | Registry extract, representative identity check |
| Representative | As for a natural person plus proof of authority | Mandate document |

Verification is completed before the account is activated. A second analyst checks high-tier business files before activation.

## 4. Purpose and nature of the relationship
Onboarding records the purpose of the account and the expected activity in the customer file.

## 5. Risk classification
The scoring model assigns a tier (standard or high). High-tier files require approval by the Head of Onboarding and are referred to the EDD and PEP procedure.

## 6. If due diligence cannot be completed
The account is not opened and no transaction is carried out. For an existing customer the relationship is reviewed for termination. Compliance assesses whether the case must be reported under the suspicious-transaction reporting procedure.

## 7. Ongoing due diligence
- Standard tier: file refresh every 36 months.
- High tier: file refresh every 12 months.

## 8. Records and quality assurance
All documents and decisions are stored in the customer file and kept as set out in the record keeping policy. The KYC quality lead samples files each month.

# Enhanced due diligence and PEP procedure

## 1. Purpose and scope
This procedure applies to customers classified as high risk and to politically exposed persons (PEPs), their family members and known close associates.

## 2. When enhanced due diligence is required
Enhanced due diligence applies when the risk tier is high, when screening identifies a PEP, or when a transaction is complex, unusually large or has no apparent economic purpose.

> TO ANSWER: Which further situations does CF Bank treat as automatic EDD triggers, and who confirms them?

- Additional information on the customer and the purpose of the relationship.
- Verification of source of funds.
- Enhanced ongoing monitoring with a shorter review cycle.

## 4. Identifying PEPs

## 5. Senior management approval

## 6. Family members and close associates
> TO ANSWER: How are family members and known close associates identified, and which PEP measures apply to them?

## 7. Decision records

> Demo document for the fictional CF Bank. Illustrative content only, not legal advice.

# Sanctions screening procedure

## 1. Purpose and scope
How CF Bank screens customers, beneficial owners, representatives, counterparties and payment parties against targeted financial sanctions and other restrictive measures.

## 2. Lists
- The Union consolidated lists and the applicable national lists are loaded into the screening engine.
- Payments Operations confirms each list update has been applied within one working day.

## 3. When screening happens
| Event | Screening |
|---|---|
| Onboarding | All parties, before activation |
| Ongoing | Full rescreen of the customer base weekly |
| Payments | Every incoming and outgoing payment before release |

## 4. Alert handling
1. The first-line analyst reviews the alert within one working day and records the evidence.
2. A potential true match is escalated to the Compliance Officer immediately, and the payment is released only after review.
3. Only the Compliance Officer can confirm a match and decide on freezing and reporting.
4. A second analyst reviews closures on request.

## 5. Evasion risk and tuning
Compliance assesses the risk of non-implementation and evasion of sanctions as part of the business-wide risk assessment. Matching thresholds are changed only after testing and Compliance Officer approval.

## 6. Records
Screening results, alert decisions and list versions are kept as set out in the record keeping policy.

> Demo document for the fictional CF Bank. Illustrative content only, not legal advice.

# Suspicious transaction reporting procedure

## 1. Purpose
How any employee of CF Bank escalates a suspicion and how the Compliance Officer assesses and reports it.

## 2. Raising a suspicion
Any employee who knows, suspects or has reasonable grounds to suspect that funds are the proceeds of criminal activity or are related to terrorist financing raises an internal report the same working day, whatever the amount. This includes attempted transactions and cases where due diligence could not be completed.

## 3. Assessment
The Compliance Officer assesses the facts against everything the bank knows about the customer, including the risk profile and the expected activity, and records the assessment and its rationale, whether or not a report follows.

## 4. Decision and filing
- The Compliance Officer decides whether to report and transmits the report to the FIU.
- The filing reference is recorded in the case.

## 5. Requests from the FIU
FIU requests for information are logged on receipt with their deadline and answered by the Compliance Officer. The log is reviewed monthly.

## 6. Holding transactions
Where a transaction is suspected to be related to criminal proceeds, it is not carried out until the report is submitted and any instructions from the FIU have been followed.

## 7. No disclosure
Employees must not tell the customer or any other third person that a transaction is being assessed or that a report has been or will be made.

## 8. Records and reporting
Assessments and reports are kept as set out in the record keeping policy. The Compliance Officer reports volumes to management each year.

> Demo document for the fictional CF Bank. Illustrative content only, not legal advice.

# Record keeping and retention policy

## 1. Purpose
What CF Bank keeps, in what form, for how long, and how it produces and deletes records.

## 2. Records kept
- Copies of documents and information obtained in customer due diligence.
- The assessment of every suspicion and any report to the FIU, whether or not a report was made.
- Supporting evidence and records of transactions.
- Payer and payee information that accompanies transfers of funds.

Records are kept unredacted.

## 3. Retention
| Record | Retention | Starts |
|---|---|---|
| Customer due diligence file | 5 years | End of the business relationship |
| Occasional transaction file | 5 years | Date of the transaction |
| Transfer information | 5 years | Date of the transfer |
| Suspicion assessments and reports | 5 years | Date of the assessment |

The Head of Compliance confirms yearly whether national law requires a longer period for any record type.

## 4. Deletion
When the retention period ends, personal data is deleted unless another legal basis requires it to be kept. Technology confirms deletion in writing.

## 5. Producing records
Compliance is the single contact point for the FIU and supervisors. Enquiries about whether the bank has had a relationship with a person during the last five years are answered through the secure channel.

## 6. Security and access
Access to records is limited by role and logged. Records cannot be altered after storage.

> Demo document for the fictional CF Bank. Illustrative content only, not legal advice.

# ICT risk and operational resilience policy

## 1. Purpose and scope
How CF Bank manages ICT risk and keeps critical and important functions available. It forms part of the overall risk management system.

## 2. Management body responsibilities
The Executive Committee approves and reviews this policy, the digital operational resilience strategy, the ICT business continuity policy, the ICT audit plan, the ICT budget and the policy on ICT third-party services. It receives a yearly report on major incidents.

## 3. ICT risk management framework
- The Head of Technology manages and oversees ICT risk.
- Risk, control and internal audit functions are kept separate.
- The framework is documented and reviewed at least once a year and after any major incident.

## 4. Identification
Technology maintains an inventory of ICT-supported business functions and assets, classifies them, and reviews the classification at least yearly.

## 5. Protection, detection and response
| Area | Owner | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| Access control | Platform engineering | Role-based, reviewed quarterly |
| Monitoring and alerts | Platform engineering | 24x7 alerting with defined thresholds |
| Business continuity | Head of Technology | Plans tested yearly |
| Backup and restore | Platform engineering | Restore tested yearly |

## 6. Incident management
All ICT incidents are recorded and classified by severity and criticality of the services affected. The Head of Technology decides whether an incident is major; Compliance notifies the competent authority.

## 7. Resilience testing
Vulnerability scans run twice a year.

|---|---|---|
| Access control | Platform engineering | Role-based, reviewed quarterly |
| Monitoring and alerts | Platform engineering | 24x7 alerting with defined thresholds |
| Business continuity | Head of Technology | Plans tested yearly |
| Backup and restore | Platform engineering | Restore tested twice a year |

## 6. Incident management
All ICT incidents are recorded and classified by severity and criticality of the services affected. The Head of Technology decides whether an incident is major; Compliance notifies the competent authority.

## 7. Resilience testing
An annual testing programme covers vulnerability scans, scenario tests and penetration testing. Findings are tracked until closed.

## 8. Learning
After every major incident a review identifies causes and improvements; results are fed back into this framework.

> Demo document for the fictional CF Bank. Illustrative content only, not legal advice.

# Outsourcing and third-party risk policy

## 1. Purpose and scope
How CF Bank decides what to outsource, contracts for it, monitors providers and plans exits. It covers ICT services, AML/CFT tasks and agents.

## 2. Principles
- CF Bank remains fully responsible for the services it outsources.
- Every arrangement is classified as supporting a critical or important function or not.
- The management body reviews the risk of arrangements supporting critical or important functions at least yearly.

## 3. Register
The Head of Technology keeps a register of all contractual arrangements for ICT services. Arrangements that support critical or important functions are distinguished. The register is provided to the competent authority on request.

## 4. Before contracting
1. Classify the arrangement.
2. Identify and assess the risks, including concentration risk.
3. Run due diligence on the provider and check information security standards.
4. Identify conflicts of interest.
5. Obtain approval from the Executive Committee for critical or important functions.

## 5. Contracts
Contracts follow the bank's checklist, which includes service descriptions, locations of processing, data protection, access and recovery, service levels, audit rights and termination rights.

## 6. AML/CFT tasks
AML/CFT tasks may be outsourced only after the supervisor has been notified. Approval of policies, the risk profile of a customer, the decision to enter a relationship, reporting to the FIU and approval of detection criteria stay in-house, subject to the exceptions in the law.

## 7. Monitoring and exit
Each provider is reviewed at least yearly, and critical providers at least twice a year. Exit plans exist for every provider supporting a critical or important function.

# AML/CFT training and awareness standard

## 1. Objective
Everyone who needs to apply AML/CFT requirements understands them, the bank's risks and its procedures.

## 2. Audience
All employees, plus agents and distributors, complete the core course. Role-based modules apply to Onboarding, Payments Operations, Compliance, Customer Support and the Executive Committee.

## 3. Frequency
- Core course within 60 days of joining.
- Refresher every 12 months.
- Targeted session after a material change in procedures or risk.

## 4. Documentation
Compliance records attendance, results and content versions. Records are kept as set out in the record keeping policy.

## 5. Assessment of staff
Staff in AML/CFT roles are assessed for skills, knowledge, good repute and integrity before they start and at regular intervals.

## 6. Reminders
Compliance emails staff who have not completed the core course.
